thread.title: BlackBerry (BB) 1st Quarter Earnings: What to Expect

author: Richard Saintvilus
title: BlackBerry (BB) 1st Quarter Earnings: What to Expect
text:
Shutterstock photo
BlackBerry ( BB ) is set to report first quarter fiscal 2019 earnings results before the opening bell Friday.
This once-iconic smartphone maker, which pioneered the mobile computing market, has turned itself into a security-focused enterprise software company. And while many pundits have doubted BlackBerry’s survivability, the question has now turned to whether the Canadian tech giant can turn its new and growing customer base into a recurring revenue stream.
The company’s Software & Services business, which in 2016 accounted for just 24% of total revenue, now accounts for 81% of its total revenue as of the end of fiscal 2018. And that number has grown from 50% in 2017. The key for BlackBerry’s success going forward and, ultimately its arrival as an Enterprise-of-Things entity, would require for that number to keep climbing.
Given that corporations are constantly in need of security solutions for their growing number of network-connected devices, BlackBerry has carved out a nice niche for what it calls the fifth wave of enterprise productivity. BlackBerry management forecasts the number of connected devices to surge more than 600% in the next three years, rising from 6.4 billion connected devices in 2017 to 46 billion by the end of 2021. That’s a compound annual growth rate of 56%.
The company believes it has an enormous opportunity to services customers in need of device security as the number of connected devices grow over the next several years, especially given the rate at which cyberattacks on mobile and traditional devices have grown recently. But BlackBerry still has a long way to go to earn Wall Street’s trust.
The company, which conceded the mobile hardware market to Apple ( AAPL ) and Samsung ( SSNLF ), must figure out a way to get revenue growing again. Of the five analysts tracking BlackBerry stock, only two have assigned Buy recommendation, while two rates it a Hold. The last recommendation is a Sell. Can Friday’s earnings and guidance win some brownie points?
For the quarter that ended May, analysts expect BlackBerry to report breakeven adjusted earnings per share on revenue of $209.34 million. This compares to the year-ago quarter when earnings were 2 cents per share on $244 million in revenue. For the full year, ending in February, earnings are projected to be 6 cents per share, down from 14 cents a year ago, while revenue of $886.61 million would decline 8.3% year over year.
With revenue for both the quarter and full year projected to decline, it’s tough to make a close-to-accurate prediction of where BlackBerry’s profits will be, thus speculate on the stock. What’s more, the company would need to make some sizable investments (spending) to get analysts excited. And that’s a double-edged sword for investors who would much rather see the bottom line grow.
In other words, while the company has successfully transitioned away from hardware to software, BlackBerry is still a wait-and-see story.
